b: On the verge of her debut solo album, Radie Peat of Lankum and ØXN presents 13 records that have held sway over her life and work, from Nico to Beak >

Radie Peat is rightly known as a generational talent in traditional folk music. With all-conquering Lankum and doomy supergroup ØXN (with Katie Kim, Eleanor Myler and John ‘Spud’ Murphy) she has proved herself as dazzling an instrumentalist (playing concertina, accordion, harmonium, tin whistle and much more) as she is a singer; her voice never fails to imbue her material with an elemental power.

Peat’s masterful debut solo album No Human Tongue Can Tell, centred on songs united by themes of female struggle and endurance, only furthers that status. Aside from a few drum and string contributions, she challenged herself to play every instrument. It was part of a concerted effort, she tells us, to push past her limitations, and in doing so to keep pushing at the boundaries of what’s possible in traditional music.

And yet, anyone even half-familiar with Peat’s work knows that however deep her roots in folk, she draws her power from broader sources too. Her Baker’s Dozen doesn’t just reflect her love of trad. There are the experimental and electronic records that taught her the value of music that builds slowly and then releases; the albums that show the art of perfect production; and music so weird that it sounds like nothing else on earth. It’s a broad range, but whether sonically or philosophically you can find the DNA of all of them at the core of her own work.

It’s also notable that so many of Peat’s choices are the product of friends and contemporaries or were introduced to her by bandmates during long van journeys while touring. Many of the Irish records here have received far less attention than Lankum, or were released before the press cottoned on to the excitement of the country’s latest so-called ‘folk revival’. It’s proof, she says, phoning in during a rare moment of downtime amid the bustle of No Human Tongue…’s launch, that the zeitgeist can paint a false picture. “I reject that word ‘revival’,” she says. “It makes it seems like we needed to revive something, whereas it never went away. From the outsider perspective it’s become more commercially popular or in the public eye, but from within it it just feels like a continuation.”

And yet, Peat feels like her Baker’s Dozen still doesn’t scratch the surface. “This is an extremely hard thing to do,” she says. “As soon as I submitted the list to you I was kicking myself about all the other things that I should have put on.” Throughout our chat, one tangent or another will remind her suddenly of another favourite and she’ll sound genuinely gutted by its exclusion. Particularly honourable mentions go to Joanna Newsom’s The Milk-Eyed Mender, Sibylle Baier’s Colour Green, Brian Eno’s Another Green World, and the entire discography of Jim White.
Radie Peat’s debut solo album No Human Tongue Can Tell is released on 13 November via Rough Trade.
